chunks: "I want them straight where I can and, when they have to turn, 45 degree mitred corners or smooth curves, never a sharp 90 and never an acute angle.
Constant width, no stubs, no T-junctions, and any width change as a gradual taper. The reason is that the impedance of a trace depends on its width over the plane.

At a square 90 degree corner, the copper momentarily gets about 40% wider along the diagonal, so you get a bit of extra capacitance, so the impedance dips for a few picoseconds and part of the edge reflects.
I actually worked the number: for a 50 ohm line that's on the order of ten femtofarads, which is a reflection of well under 1% with a 100 picoseconds edge.
So at modest speeds a right angle is not what kills your board.

But it only costs me a mouse click to route 45 degrees, it's honest good practice at multi-gigabit speeds where edges are 20 or 30 picoseconds, and it avoids acute angles that trap etchant at the fab.

The shapes that really hurt are stubs, wide pads on a narrow trace, and tapers that are too abrupt, so I pay more attention to those: teardrops where a trace meets a pad, symmetric bends on differential pairs, and a smooth fan-out."
